standard.title: Sustainable use of resources
standard.description: sustainable use and management of renewable and non-renewable resources, including the custodial responsibility First Nations Australians have for Country/Place
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS4K05: Students explained the importance of environments and vegetation to people and animals. From Y3 (AC9HS3K06): Students explored rules and community responsibility.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how resources can be used and managed sustainably, including First Nations Australian custodial responsibility for Country/Place.

nodes.label: Renewable and non-renewable resources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between renewable and non-renewable resources and describe sustainable and non-sustainable ways resources are used.
nodes.minimum_width: Classify at least four resources as renewable or non-renewable and describe one sustainable and one non-sustainable use.
nodes.typical_width: Explore how resources are used sustainably and non-sustainably (auditing classroom use, recycling, waste disposal, managing timber); distinguish renewable from non-renewable; investigate local recycling and waste systems.
wider: Audit resource use in the school and propose sustainable alternatives for the least sustainable practices
Research how a specific renewable resource (timber, water) is managed in Australia and evaluate whether the management is sustainable
nodes.hinge_reason: The renewable/non-renewable distinction underpins all sustainability analysis — without it, students cannot evaluate whether specific practices are sustainable.

response_modes.reason: Renewable vs non-renewable is a conceptual distinction requiring clear criteria — use concrete examples and classification exercises before sustainability analysis.

success_criteria: Classifies at least four resources as renewable or non-renewable
Describes one sustainable and one non-sustainable use of resources

nodes.label: First Nations Australian custodial responsibility
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how First Nations Australians have practised sustainable resource use through knowledge and practices linked to custodial responsibility for Country/Place.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least one First Nations Australian practice of sustainable resource use and explain how it demonstrates custodial responsibility.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate how First Nations Australians adapted sustainable resource use through rotational harvesting, fire management, endemic plant use for food/shelter/medicine/tools, and how this knowledge is transmitted through stories and songs.
wider: Compare First Nations Australian sustainable land management practices (e.g. fire, rotational use) with contemporary conservation practices and discuss complementarities
Investigate how a specific First Nations Australian sustainable practice (e.g. mutton-bird harvesting in Tasmania) works in detail

response_modes.reason: Multiple First Nations Australian sustainable practices from different regions reveal the breadth and sophistication of Indigenous land management across Australia.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations Australian sustainable practices offer genuinely different models of resource management grounded in 65,000+ years of ecological knowledge — this is one of the most significant widening opportunities in the Year 4 curriculum.
success_criteria: Describes at least one First Nations Australian sustainable resource practice
Explains how it demonstrates custodial responsibility for Country/Place
